content: A study by Duchesne et al. demonstrated a significant reduction in the cost of viral load testing for patients, decreasing from $170 to $28 per test. This was achieved by repurposing existing GeneXpert technology, originally designed for HIV diagnostics, for hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing. The study utilized a decision tree model to evaluate 12 testing strategies in Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Senegal. These strategies included point-of-care (PoC) anti-HCV tests combined with PoC RNA tests, as well as strategies using only PoC RNA tests. While the specific PoC RNA platforms were not identified, both GeneXpert and GeneDrive systems were referenced. The 2018 cost data were sourced from reference laboratories in these countries and existing literature. Notably, the strategy using only PoC RNA tests resulted in 185 false positives, compared to fewer than four false positives with other strategies. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio increased when accounting for patient loss to follow-up due to reluctance to undergo venipuncture, highlighting the superiority of the combined PoC anti-HCV and HCV-RNA strategy. However, the cost per additional true positive case identified remained high for these settings. Importantly, the studies did not evaluate cost-effectiveness in terms of broader health outcomes, such as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). The evidence for PoC RNA assays versus laboratory-based assays was graded as low certainty due to the absence of randomized controlled trials and reliance on observational studies. This review is the first global analysis to assess the effectiveness of PoC HCV viral load testing, a promising diagnostic tool to improve access to confirmatory testing for viremia and subsequent treatment. The analysis included 45 observational studies (64 study arms) that used PoC HCV RNA assays, with data on key outcomes across the HCV care cascade, such as RNA testing, treatment uptake, and turnaround times. Twelve studies included direct comparisons with laboratory-based assays, providing more robust evidence. Key findings included significantly shorter turnaround times with PoC assays (median 5 days) compared to laboratory-based PoC assays (64 days) or high-throughput RNA assays (67 days). Treatment uptake was also higher with PoC assays, reaching 77% for onsite testing and 81% for mobile PoC testing, compared to 53% with laboratory-based assays. The greatest improvements in RNA testing and treatment uptake were observed among people who inject drugs, homeless populations, and prisoners. Direct comparisons consistently showed lower turnaround times in PoC assay arms. The impact of PoC assays was most pronounced when integrated into simplified care models, where testing and treatment occurred at the same site and, ideally, on the same day. Mobile units deploying PoC assays effectively targeted hard-to-reach populations, achieving short turnaround times and minimizing patient loss through the care cascade. Cost-effectiveness analyses in prisons in England, among people who inject drugs in Senegal, and in general populations in Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Senegal consistently found PoC RNA assays to be cost-effective compared to non-PoC assays. However, these studies often assessed cost-effectiveness per true positive diagnosis, potentially overlooking downstream benefits such as reduced loss to follow-up. A complementary systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies evaluated the diagnostic performance of PoC HCV RNA assays versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of PoC assays were both 99%, comparable to laboratory-based standards, across diverse settings and populations in both lowand high-income countries. This review had several strengths, including rigorous stratification of studies by care models and the inclusion of direct within-study comparisons. However, limitations included a lack of randomized controlled trials, reliance on observational data, and high heterogeneity in care models and study populations. Many studies lacked data on all relevant cascade outcomes, and some were based on interim results. Despite these limitations, strong associations were observed between PoC assays and improved outcomes. The findings align with World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for PoC RNA assays in other infectious diseases, such as HIV and tuberculosis, where their use has been associated with faster diagnosis and treatment initiation. These principles can be extended to HCV, supporting the use of PoC platforms to simplify care pathways and improve outcomes. Policy implications include the need to scale up PoC HCV viral load testing to achieve global HCV elimination targets. WHO guidelines already recommend strategies to enhance hepatitis testing and linkage to care, such as peer workers and integrated services. This review provides evidence to support the inclusion of PoC HCV viral load platforms in decentralized, co-located testing and treatment models, particularly in settings like harm-reduction sites, primary care, prisons, and HIV clinics. Future research should focus on methodologically rigorous comparative studies, ideally randomized controlled trials, to evaluate PoC platforms for HCV and HBV diagnosis and treatment decisions. Evaluations should capture outcomes across the entire care continuum, including costs, to enable comprehensive cost-effectiveness analyses. Fully decentralized HCV care models, where testing and treatment are integrated at the same site, are critical to improving access and uptake, especially for vulnerable populations. Multi-disease testing platforms, such as GeneXpert, offer opportunities for integration and cost savings, particularly in settings with existing infrastructure for HIV or TB testing.
